We don’t need another reason to love creativity, but research linking arts participation to slower biological aging is a pretty good one. 🎨 A recent University College London study found that more frequent engagement in arts and cultural activities was associated with slower biological aging. Weekly arts participants showed a 4% slower pace of aging than those who rarely participated. Here’s why this matters for play. Art is one way we play. When we paint, dance, make music, experiment with materials, or create something alongside others, we’re engaging in the very things that make play powerful: curiosity, imagination, expression, and exploration. The research gives us another reason to take these experiences seriously. Play isn’t just entertainment or a break from real life. It’s part of how we nurture our creativity, connection, and vitality. Make something. Move something. Try something new. Give yourself the gift ofplay. #PlayIntention #PowerOfPlay #CreativeWellbeing #ArtsAndHealt

posts.c: One of the densest concentrations of geysers in Yellowstone can be found in the remote Shoshone Geyser Basin, on the west side of Shoshone Lake. We visit the area in the latest Yellowstone Volcano Observatory monthly video update. 🌊 Shoshone Geyser Basin is one of the most spectacular in all of Yellowstone National Park. Located deep in the backcountry along the west side of Shoshone Lake, the area has one of the densest concentrations of geysers, second only to the Upper Geyser Basin (where Old Faithful is located). There are over 100 geysers in this region and 40 or 50 might be active at any given time. A trail takes you right by Minute Man geyser (always at the ready!), so it is quite easy to watch the frequent eruptions there. ⚡During the month of October 2026, the University of Utah Seismograph Stations, which monitors and operates the Yellowstone seismic network, located 66 earthquakes. The largest was a Magnitude 2.0. Throughout 2026, there has been very little change in ground

posts.c: A little throwback to my broke college girl dinner era…. Honestly, I forgot how good these things are. Basically everything you want in a pizza, minus having to make an actual pizza. And yes, they’re still just as good as they were at 1AM in college. Here’s how I made them: - Split English muffins in half, drizzle with EVOO, sprinkle with garlic powder, and bake at 400°F for about 10–12 minutes, until lightly golden. - Add marinara, mozzarella, provolone, dried oregano, and a little garlic salt. - Back into the oven until the cheese is melted and bubbly. - Serve with extra warm marinara for dipping. Please tell me I’m not the only one who lived on these back in the day….

posts.c: 🌳Come tree planting with VJ Comai, @btvparks City Arborist and crew! The team is finishing up a massive effort to replant hundreds of trees in City greenbelts this fall, following the removal of the City’s Ash trees that were struck by the Emerald Ash Borer. The Ash Borer is an invasive insect that causes die off in Ash trees within a couple of years of being infested. The trees team has been inter-planting new trees over the past 8 years to prepare for the canopy loss and is now finishing up planting in areas that did not allow for planting prior to Ash removal. Thank you to the crews for caring for and managing Burlington’s urban tree canopy — a vital resource for the environment in our generation and many to come! Thank you to @branchoutburlington for supporting this effort! Learn more at the link in our bio!

posts.c: Hidden beauty 💛 Agorastos Papatsanis (@agorastospapatsanis) uses ultraviolet light to reveal the glowing yellow stems of beautiful bonnet mushrooms growing from a decaying log. On the lower slopes of Greece’s Mount Olympus, Agorastos experimented with ultraviolet (UV) illumination until it revealed the strongest fluorescent response from these mushrooms known as ‘beautiful bonnets’. While humans cannot see UV light, we can get an inkling of its effect, thanks to the phenomenon of fluorescence. Mycologists are harnessing this phenomenon to distinguish closely related species of fungi by the colours and patterns they reveal under UV. 📸 'Shedding Light' is the winner of #WPY62's Plants and Fungi category. See all 100 winning images in our new exhibition! Book your tickets via the link in our bio now. #WPY #WildlifePhotographerOfTheYear #WildlifePhotography #NaturePhotography #NaturalHistoryMuseum

posts.c: November is Native American Heritage Month, a time to honor the histories, cultures, traditions, and contributions of Indigenous peoples. This month provides an opportunity to learn about and celebrate the rich heritage of Native communities while recognizing their enduring impact on our nation. We honor tribal sovereignty and acknowledge the many contributions Indigenous peoples have made in areas ranging from the arts and education to public service and military service. As we reflect on our country's history, we recognize both the challenges and achievements that have shaped Indigenous communities. This month, we honor the past, celebrate the present, and look toward a future where Indigenous cultures, traditions, and communities continue to thrive. #nativeamericanheritagemonth #representationmatters #inclusion #belonging #btv #reib

posts.c: In this final video in our explainer series about the new deer hunting regulations this year, our Deer and Moose Project Leader Nick Fortin and Sergeant Dana Joyal from the Vermont Warden Service break down what is needed to legally take a doe in the upcoming rifle season. In order to legally take a doe during rifle season, you must have received an antlerless permit designated for a specific wildlife management unit (WMU). If you do not have a permit, you may not take a doe during the rifle season. If a hunter is unsuccessful during the rifle season, they may use that antlerless permit during the conventional muzzleloader season. Visit our website for more information about taking a doe during rifle season and all the new deer regulation changes.

posts.c: Día de los Muertos has its roots in an Aztec ritual known as Miccaihuitl, honoring those who have passed. The celebration coincides with the return of monarch butterflies that typically flutter away from our region and make the long flight back to Mexico to spend their winter in a warmer climate. Believed to carry the souls of the departed returning to visit their families, it’s easy to see why these beautiful, winged messengers are held sacred by so many Indigenous communities along their path. 🌼🌼🌼 El Día de los Muertos tiene sus raíces en un antiguo ritual Azteca llamado Miccaihuitl, en honor de los antepasados. Da la casualidad de que coincide con el retorno de las mariposas monarcas que típicamente vuelan de nuestra región al norte y emprenden el largo vuelo de regreso a México donde pasan el invierno en un clima más cálido. Se cree que llevan consigo las almas de los difuntos que vuelven a visitar a sus familias. Es fácil ver por qué estas mensajeras aladas se consideran sagradas

While observing them, I realised that each zebra had its own family of red billed ox peckers on its back. The birds weren’t feeding, and looked quite wet from the rain that had just come, so it seemed like they were just resting there. I really liked the moment, resulting in me capturing the oxpeckers perched on the zebra’s back for ‘Stripes and Feathers’." - Oscar Whitfield Oscar is a young photographer who grew up in Zimbabwe and still travels home in his school holidays, during which he spends a lot of time in Zambezi National Park. posts.c: I wish they had the slightest idea that how much they mean to us. Just yesterday, one of our cats disappeared out of sight for a few minutes as I’d left her chilling in the backyard. These are indoor cats, so they have absolutely zero clue about life beyond the four walls of our home & the little garden they know so well. And in those few moments, I went through an entire range of emotions. From panic to worry, from imagining all sorts of terrible possibilities to the fear of not knowing where she had gone. Meanwhile, 🐈 walked back in, completely unbothered, after her antics. 🤦🏻‍♀️ Also, as a cat owner, if there’s one thing I could recommend, it would be investing in a self-cleaning litter box. It has genuinely changed our lives, especially in a multi-cat household. Ours is a pretty old model, so it’s too big compared to the much smarter ones available these days. 🤌🏼 - - - #livingroom #bedroom #bluebedroom #cosybedroom #bedroomideas

posts.c: Have you seen a whale shark before? Alex Lindbloom’s (@alexlindbloomphoto) photo shows a whale shark investigating the catch of a 'bagan', or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua. He used the lights of the began to illuminate the sharks for his drone’s camera. Local fishing communities are using the predictable occurrence of whale sharks at bagans to attract tourists. Although contact with bagans can cause some minor injuries to whale sharks, this isn’t a major cause of mortality. Instead, the main reasons for the sharp decline in whale sharks in the Indo-Pacific region over the past 75 years are ship strikes, entanglements with fishing gear and illegal fishing. 📸 ‘Night-Time Catch’ is the winner of #WPY62's Oceans: The Bigger Picture category. Book your tickets for #WPY62 now via the link in our bio! #WPY #WildlifePhotographerOfTheYear #WildlifePhotography #NaturePhotography #NaturalHistoryMuseum #WhaleShark

posts.c: Star Wars became hugely popular because it combined an exciting adventure story with groundbreaking special effects. When George Lucas released the first film in 1977, audiences had rarely seen space battles, alien worlds, and futuristic technology portrayed so convincingly. Its memorable characters, including Luke Skywalker, Darth Vader, and Princess Leia, helped make the story appealing to audiences of all ages. Another major reason was its enormous cultural influence. Star Wars introduced iconic lightsabers, unforgettable music by John Williams, and a fictional universe that fans could explore through toys, books, games, and sequels. Its simple story of good versus evil made it easy to connect with, while its detailed universe kept fans interested for decades. It transformed science fiction from a relatively niche genre into mainstream entertainment. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: In celebration of Native American Heritage Month, we’re honored to share the powerful words and artistry of Joy Harjo, a citizen of the Muscogee (Creek) Nation and the first Native American to serve as United States Poet Laureate. Last year, we had the privilege of welcoming @joyharjoforreal to Longwood for a two-week residency as the inaugural recipient of our André Harvey Creative Fellowship. Rooted in Muscogee traditions and a lifetime of fearless creativity, she brought a powerful new voice to our landscapes and gifted us with a deeply moving presentation that includes reflections and readings from her award-winning body of work. We’re grateful for the wisdom, artistry, and perspective Harjo brought to Longwood, and delighted to share this special experience with you. 📽️ Watch the full presentation at the 🔗 in our bio. 📸 Carlos Alejandro

posts.c: Hats were once an essential part of everyday fashion because they served both practical and social purposes. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, men and women wore hats to protect themselves from sunlight, rain, and cold weather. Hats also symbolized respectability, social status, and good manners. Going outside without one was sometimes considered improper, especially on formal occasions. Hat-wearing declined dramatically during the mid-20th century as fashion became more casual, cars became widespread, and elaborate hairstyles grew popular. President John F. Kennedy is sometimes blamed for ending the hat trend, although it was already declining before his presidency. Interestingly, there was a time when leaving home without a hat could seem almost as unusual as leaving without shoes today. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: A volunteer effort to fix the public ice rink in Barre was successful, and the rink will open this weekend as scheduled. The city had said last month that the BOR Arena would not open this year due to mechanical problems. But then, about a dozen volunteers stepped up to try to get the ice-making equipment working for one more season. City Manager Patrick Cushing says the repairs are holding. "It shows the importance of this thing that it bridged municipal lines. It bridged economic lines," Cushing said. "Everyone just came together and said, ‘We need this ice rink for the kids. We need this for the community.'" The volunteers, and the community, donated about $50,000 in equipment and time to get the rink in shape. Cushing says the fix will hopefully get them through this season, but longer term structural issues at the rink will need to be addressed. Video courtesy of Trym Chouinard

posts.c: Pirates were far more organized than movies suggest, especially during the Golden Age of Piracy between the 1650s and 1730s. Many pirate crews elected their captains, voted on important decisions, and followed written rules. Some even had compensation systems for injured crew members. Interestingly, pirates rarely buried treasure, and the famous practice of making prisoners walk the plank was much less common than Hollywood suggests. Another surprising fact is that pirates sometimes used intimidation to avoid fighting altogether. The famous skull-and-crossbones flag, known as the Jolly Roger, warned ships to surrender before an attack. Pirates also included women, such as Anne Bonny and Mary Read, who became notorious in the early 18th century. Despite their reputation for lawlessness, some pirate crews operated with surprisingly democratic rules, at least among their own members. Like this content? Follow us for more @dadsaysjokes ❤️

posts.c: The stars are just the night sky's mice... The first image is Webb's near-infrared view of the Cat's Head Nebula, a star-forming region. Webb can see through the opaque clouds of dust and gas to see the stars forming within. One of these makes up the cat's glowing "eye" and another, with Webb's characteristic eight-pointed diffraction spikes, its whiskers. The second slide shows Webb's mid-infrared look at the Cat's head, the dust shining brightly. There are structures to the left of the cat visible in the infrared that do not appear in @NASAHubble's visible light view (third slide). The cat's eye is reddish here, glowing from inside the dust. The bright yellow ridge along the cat's "chest" shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. Happy Halloween! Credits: Image: NASA, ESA, STScI; Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI) Read more at the link in our bio. Image description in comments.

A big yawn mid-stretch makes for a deceptive image. Most of us are aware that wolves do not impersonate grannies to trick children or huff and puff houses to the ground. Still, the archetype of the “big bad wolf” persists in folklore and fiction. Fairy tales like Little Red Riding Hood seem harmless enough, but as biodiversity plummets across the world, suddenly the fictitious villain becomes a very real and very convenient scapegoat. When local wildlife begins to decline, predators are often unfairly blamed for the loss, despite the fact that habitat destruction and development play a much larger role. My hope in sharing the beauty of animals like wolves in my new book Reverence is to inspire empathy and encourage us to reevaluate how we coexist with our planet’s predators. posts.c: Product reviews have a powerful influence on what people buy, with many shoppers trusting feedback from strangers almost as much as personal recommendations. Interestingly, products with a few negative reviews can sometimes appear more trustworthy than those with nothing but perfect ratings, because a flawless review history may seem suspicious. Another surprising fact is that people are more likely to leave reviews after extremely good or bad experiences than after ordinary ones. This can make online ratings less representative of the average customer’s experience. Fake reviews also complicate matters, which is why a detailed, balanced three-star review can sometimes tell you more than dozens of enthusiastic five-star ratings. Like this content? posts.c: When Halloween is over, look for Dracula in a hibernaculum! A hibernaculum is a place like a cave, den, or burrow, where animals seek shelter for the winter. At least 10 of Yellowstone’s 13 species of bats are winter hibernators. In the greater Yellowstone area, there are few known hibernacula, though researchers have identified some within the park. More surprising is that researchers have documented bat activity in Northern Yellowstone throughout the winter, despite little insect activity, and freezing cold temperatures. #BatWeek

posts.c: Happy Hubble Halloween! This new image of the Cat's Head Nebula shows a star-forming region with an eerily feline resemblance. The distinctive “cat’s head” shape of the nebula was likely sculpted over time by the intense ultraviolet radiation and winds from massive stars in the Carina Nebula, within which this nebula resides. Dare to learn more at the link in our bio! Image description: Visible-light image of the Cat’s Head Nebula by the Hubble Space Telescope. A dark brown, opaque filament of dust is in the center, stretching from the bottom to almost the very top. It has a narrow, irregular shape that resembles a cat sitting with its back toward the viewer and a tail extending downward. The cat’s head is turned toward the right, revealing a red glowing eye. The top half of the background is bright blue. posts.c: Since the founding of the city, Parisians had been burying their dead in the middle of town, which led to an untenable situation: In the spring of 1780, heavy rains wrecked a burial mound at the overcrowded Les Innocents cemetery, sending a wave of decaying corpses tumbling into the building next door. The king’s solution to necrotic overpopulation? Shut down all of Paris’s graveyards and transfer all the bodies to an extensive network of underground tunnels left behind by 13th-century limestone miners—a task that took 12 years to complete. Today, morbid-minded tourists—like our @cntraveler editorial operations manager, @tayloreisenhauer, who captured these photos—can visit @catacombesdeparis_officiel. There, you can explore about a mile of this underground labyrinth’s 200 miles of bone-lined walls, greeted by this friendly inscription: "Arrête! C'est ici l'empire de la mort" (Stop! This is the empire of death).
posts.hd: Paris catacombs built from moved cemetery bones

posts.c: Someone tell Belle I found her library in Vermont. 📚♥️ The @stjohnsburyathenaeum is straight out of Beauty and the Beast, with ornate woodwork and spiral staircases inside a building that’s been welcoming readers for more than 150 years. It’s such an unusual find in Vermont’s Northeast Kingdom, right on Main Street, and the library is only part of the reason to visit. Horace Fairbanks gave the Athenaeum to the community in 1871, and it opened with 8,000 books. I love that it still serves as the town’s public library. Imagine getting to call this your neighborhood reading spot, with sunlight coming through those tall, arched windows while you settle into a book. Then there’s the art gallery, added in 1873, where paintings in heavy gilded frames hang one above another in a setting that preserves the feel of a 19th-century museum. Albert Bierstadt’s The Domes of the Yosemite dominates the back wall at 10 feet tall and 15 feet wide. The painting even influenced the design of the gallery it

posts.c: Our Orange County tour continues to the Cilley Bridge today. Here is another of the area's many multiple kingpost bridges. The bridge was built in 1883 and rehabilitated in 2006. The Covered Spans of Yesteryear website provides some historical background: "The bridge was named for the nearby Cilley family and was built at a cost of $523.35. When built, its portals were skewed by seven degrees; thus, it exhibits a slight camber. The truss is unusual in that the truss has an upper chord with the vertical tension members extending slightly above the chord to support the roof sill and the roof". #vtcbsinayear #cilleycbvt #tunbridgevt #vermontscoveredbridges #vermontcoveredbridgesociety #coveredspansofyesteryear https://www.vermontbridges.org/orange_county_combined-wcg-phase1_cilley.shtml

posts.c: Our Sun knows how to get in the spirit! 🎃 Years ago, our Solar Dynamics Observatory caught our Sun looking like a jack-o’-lantern, with active regions shaped like a carved face. Swipe to see other cosmic curiosities captured over the years. #NASA #Halloween #Space The wispy white gas of this star-forming cloud, Lupus 3, is 500 light-years away in the constellation Scorpius. It looks something like a wave of ectoplasm or stretch of cobwebs. Which do you see? As we set our sights on the Hourglass Nebula, it appears to gaze back at us. This creepy cosmic object is a planetary nebula, the glowing relic of a dying, Sun-like star. This ghoulish cloud of gas and dust, called the Ghost Nebula, is 550 light-years away in the constellation Cassiopeia. Its long ghostly veil is shaped by radiation from the bright stars embedded within it. This witch is busy brewing baby stars! Named the Witch Head, this nebula is found 800 light-years away in the constellation Orion, just off the hunter’s “knee.”
posts.cp: Our Sun knows how to get in the spirit!

Relive last summer’s Main Street Block Party when you take in the collaborative Community Steamroller Block Prints on view at City Hall through January 2027. ⁠ ⁠ July’s community celebration brought neighbors together to celebrate in the completion of the Great Streets: Main Street revitalization project this summer. BCA brought large-scale printmaking to the street with a little help from our friends @sdirelandvt and their full-sized steamroller. We brought together community and school groups, Main Street businesses, local artists, and the general public, to design and carve 3-by-3-foot blocks of MDF plywood. During the Block Party, community members and BCA staff helped prepare the blocks with ink before large sheets of paper were laid on top to create a printing press. posts.c: New Tools for Healthier Soils! We’ve got new equipment at the Intervale Center! Thanks to funding from the Vermont Housing and Conservation Board and the Vermont Agency of Agriculture, our new 6-foot seed drill and flail mower will make it easier to plant and manage crops across the Intervale. Right now, we are planting cover crops. Cover crops are planted to protect the soil between growing seasons, rather than for harvest. Their roots hold soil in place, build organic matter, and reduce nutrient runoff; creating a strong, resilient foundation for our food system. The seed drill plants seeds with minimal soil disturbance, and the mower chops down vegetation for quick and efficient turnover back to crop production. Their compact size makes them ideal for smaller farm fields and garden plots in the Intervale that were formerly cover cropped by hand or not at all. These tools will support Intervale Center land stewardship, Intervale farmers, the Intervale Conservation Nursery, and agrofo

posts.c: Creating my book Reverence required endless hours of slogging through over 2 million images in my digital archives. In my bleary-eyed scrolling haze, I suddenly came across images I hadn’t seen in years. The polar bear above visited my cabin in the middle of a blizzard in Svalbard, and you can see in the series how she first peeked in before pawing at the window. The third image, titled Face to Face, became one of my best known prints and is the only image of mine I have ever felt compelled to hang my home. If you’d like to hear the full story in person, please join me Saturday Nov 14th at the @iconicimagesgallery in London for a special Q&A and book signing. Tickets are available through the link in my bio.

posts.c: Halloween is a time for things that go bump in the night. National parks have plenty of those. Boo! Still with us? From mysterious noises in the woods to wildlife that would prefer you keep your distance, the great outdoors can be downright spooky after dark. But the scariest encounters often have less to do with ghosts and more to do with poor planning, questionable decisions, and the occasional tree root working in cahoots with gravity. Whether you’re hiking a shadowy trail, camping beneath a full moon, or simply enjoying the autumn scenery, a few simple precautions can help keep your adventure from becoming a horror story. Stay on marked trails, watch your step, give wildlife plenty of space, check the weather, and pack the essentials. And if something in the woods starts whispering your name? Well, perhaps don’t investigate. Good luck! NPS

posts.c: This spooky season, we're bringing you a tale of Halloween botany! The story begins with a dedicated search for the extremely rare and globally-vulnerable St. Lawrence grapefern (Sceptridium rugulosum). After weeks of combing potential habitat, one of our botanists was rewarded by finding this plant in a unique location — at the foot of a grave in a sandy cemetery in the Champlain Valley! While the location of this find is seasonally apropos, this is an exciting discovery for a more important reason: since the 90s, this species has been on the decline in Vermont. This find represents the first new population in Vermont in around 30 years, and this cemetery is currently the only known site for this rare grapefern in New England! Cemeteries often contain interesting plants that thrive in the low-competition environments created by consistent mowing as well as easy-to-dig-in sandy substrates. posts.c: A 10,000-pound bull elephant arrived yesterday and is settling into Elephant Trek! Raja came to Cincinnati from @stlzoo on a breeding recommendation from the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) Asian Elephant Species Survival Plan (SSP). He sired several calves in St. Louis but is related to all the breeding-age females there and, therefore, cannot contribute to the survival of his species there. We hope that he will hit it off with the eligible females in Cincinnati and that our herd will grow.

posts.c: You're in for a spooky trip that goes beyond your average ghost tour in New Orleans, Louisiana, known for its spiritual history, centuries-old cemeteries, French Quarter legends, and NOLA Halloween spirit, captured here by @nocturnalnola. Commerce writer @jeschapel knows the best way to do it, starting with the city's roots in voodoo: a spiritual tradition shaped by West African practices, Catholicism, and the Haitian diaspora. You can dig into the history of Marie Laveau—the legendary 19th-century voodoo practitioner whose name still pops up all over the city—at @mlhouseofvoodoo in the French Quarter. Or you can take an expert-led voodoo tour, where you'll learn all about the history and how it's ingrained in the city's culture today. @voodoomuseum can also help put the traditions into context. Be sure to also make your way to the Garden District to visit Buckner Mansion, the enormous Greek Revival house built in 1857 that American Horror Story: Coven fans will recognize as Miss Robic

Here’s looking at you, kid 👀👀👀👀 This Brazilian Whiteknee Tarantula is native to tropical areas of Brazil. Tarantula hair is adapted to help them sense vibrations and other stimuli, and some hairs are even barbed and can be used as a defensive mechanism. Many of us know tarantulas for their eight legs and two body segments, but there are other features that are characteristic of arachnids. If you look at a tarantula’s mouthparts, for instance, you will see chelicerae (jaw-like parts tipped with fangs) and a pair of pedipalps, which help them taste and hold their food. #tarantula #sandiegozoo

posts.c: Comment ‘dad’ on this post for an extra dad joke straight to your DM’s 👇 Cars use several types of filters to protect their engines, improve performance, and keep passengers comfortable. Air filters prevent dust and dirt from entering the engine, oil filters remove contaminants from engine oil, and fuel filters stop impurities from reaching the fuel system. These filters help reduce wear, improve efficiency, and extend the lifespan of important components. Cabin air filters also clean the air entering the passenger compartment, trapping dust, pollen, and other airborne particles. Interestingly, a clogged filter can reduce engine performance, restrict airflow, or cause unpleasant smells inside the car, depending on which filter is affected. Regular filter replacement is one of the simplest ways to keep a vehicle running smoothly.

posts.c: If you ask us, the longline tuna fishery in Hawaii is making waves! 🐟🌺 Solid fishery management can make even the less-selective fishing methods more ocean-friendly. Hawaii is leading the charge by making its longline fishery more environmentally sustainable. This means: ✅ switching from less than 20% human observer coverage to 100% electronic camera monitoring by 2027 to track bycatch and gather data for fishery management decisions. ✅ training fishers to safely handle and release accidentally caught species like sharks, turtles, seabirds, and marine mammals. ✅ gear modifications to reduce seabird interactions. ✅ strategic area closures to protect vulnerable species. and more! The future for longline tuna fishing in Hawaii is bright.☀️ Look for yellow- and green-rated tuna caught in Hawaii for your next sustainable meal. posts.c: What is making this sea of sand march inland? ⌛ This timelapse shows the Lençóis Maranhenses National Park in northeastern Brazil, known for its large sand dunes and seasonal rainwater lagoons. Strong winds from the Atlantic Ocean keep these dunes in constant motion. Over the years, the wind steadily pushes the sand, causing the dunes to migrate inland and change the shape of the landscape. Satellite data helps scientists track how remote landscapes change over time. Captured by the joint @nasa and @usgs Landsat program, these natural-color images show over four decades of this moving environment. Video description: A natural-color Landsat time series of Brazil’s Lençóis Maranhenses National Park spanning from 1984 to 2026. As the video plays, large white sand dunes move steadily inland across the coast. Among the shifting white sand are darker patches of seasonal rainwater lagoons and vegetation. #nasa #earth #science

posts.c: We’re not kitten around! @NASAHubble and @NASAWebb captured a purr-fect view of the Cat’s Head Nebula. This long thin structure, made of dark, dense dust, looks like the head of a cat, its eye a newborn star still shrouded by the dust and gas from which it formed. Hubble and Webb’s contrasting and complementary views give us a fuller picture of the features of this object. In the mid-infrared, as seen by Webb, the dust shines brightly while in the near-infrared, Webb can see through the dust to the stars hidden within. In visible light, Hubble's view shows a dark brown pillar of dust, with a yellow ridge along the right side. This bright rim shows gas illuminated and ionized by ultraviolet radiation from nearby massive stars. On the left are some dust pillars seen in the mid-infrared that are not observed in visible light. It's paw-sible to "fly through" these views with the help of visualizations created by (human) data scientists, which bring Hubble and Webb observations to un-fur-ge

posts.c: Burlington used to have street cars. Loads of towns and cities in Vermont had street cars. Public transit shaped the way we lived, supporting dense and walkable neighborhoods. Then on Sunday, August 4th, 1929, nearly ten thousand people packed City Hall Park to watch Burlington's last street car burn. They cheered as 20 new buses rolled down Main St. But this would not be the era of buses. It would solidify the era of the automobile. Now, 100 years later, @ridegmt faces a $3 million shortfall that threatens 30% of its service. Same as the street cars, our public transit faces an existential lack of public investment. This time, we know what happens when we light the funeral pyre, and we can't let it happen again. Take a stand for public transit. Sign the petition. Share your story. Take the bus. posts.c: 🍁 Peak fall color has entered the chat! We are officially calling it. The Gardens are gilded in autumn's incandescent glow. Golden oaks and tulip-trees light up Peirce’s Park. The Meadow Garden is a tapestry of auburn, amber, and rust. Everywhere you look, leaves and late-season blooms are reaching a glorious crescendo of color. And indoors, Chrysanthemum Festival is at peak bloom, adding an extraordinary flourish of color and artistry to the season. And like so many of nature’s most beautiful moments, this one is fleeting. Nature gives us this extraordinary spectacle and asks only that we pause long enough to appreciate it. Come see it before the leaves fall and the mums change over to Christmas! Photos by Holden Barnes, Amy Simon Berg, Hank Davis, Scott Hummel, and Becca Mathias.

posts.c: Do you know Boneyard Farm?🌱 In Fletcher, VT, first-generation farmers Hannah and John Doyle grow certified organic produce, raise sheep, and care for 180 acres of farmland and forest. Our Farm Business Services team began working alongside Hannah and John in 2019 as they planned for their future and prepared to purchase the farm in 2021. They have also collaborated with the Intervale Conservation Nursery on a riparian buffer along a stream on their farm that protects soil and water, filters runoff, and creates wildlife habitat – all essential parts of a strong, resilient food system. We loved visiting Boneyard Farm this summer and seeing how much both the business and the riparian buffer have grown. Thank you, Hannah and John, for welcoming us and for the care you bring to the land and Vermont’s food system! posts.c: Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. While El Niño occurs in the Pacific Ocean, with changes most visible along the equator, its effects can be felt all around the world. NASA satellites like PACE and Sentinel-6 are equipped to measure some of the key features of the phenomenon. Video description: Three data visualizations stacked vertically show sea surface height, sea surface temperature, and ocean color from January 2026 to September 2026. As it plays, text forms across the screen that reads “We’re experiencing a record El Niño” and transitions to “Swipe to compare the growing 2026 El Niño with a weak La Niña in 2025.” Higher waters, warmer waters, bluer waters El Niño is a natural weather pattern that occurs roughly every two to seven years and the one we’re experiencing now is on track to be the strongest on record. posts.c: It’s Pop-up week 🔍 What exactly is “slow looking”? Slow looking is an approach to viewing art that emphasizes our own observations and reflections, rather than familiarity with the artwork or art terminology. It’s also a visual thinking strategy used by first-year medical students in Dr. Sakshi Jasra’s Professionalism, Communication, and Reflection class at the Larner College of Medicine. Now in it’s third year running with the Fleming, we partnered with Dr. Jasra to transform her popular assignment into a pop-up exhibit for all! Now through Saturday, visit the Learning Studio to visit “Double Take” any time during our regular hours and try slow looking for yourself. Featuring a wide range of works from our collections, including a clay tablet from Mesopotamia, a photograph by Carrie Mae Weems, and much more, simply choose a work and follow our prompts. The only thing you need to bring is your own curiosity.

posts.c: Hardneck garlic relies on a process called vernalization, where prolonged exposure to cold temperatures triggers the physiological changes needed for proper bulb development. Without enough chilling, the plant may grow leaves but struggle to form the full, well-developed bulbs you want. Refrigerating hardneck garlic for about two months can help simulate winter, even in a warm climate. That cold exposure influences the plant’s growth signals, helping prepare it for the transition into active growth once temperatures rise. It’s essentially giving the garlic the seasonal cue it needs, without having to live somewhere with an actual winter. Once you plant those chilled cloves, they can resume growth with the cold requirement better satisfied, improving the chances of developing well-formed bulbs. It’s a great example of how understanding a plant’s biology lets you work around your climate instead of being limited by it.

posts.c: Here's something to warm your heart on a chilly fall day! These clips of a Map Turtle hatchling emerging and being released into the Missisquoi Bay were captured by our biologists as they carried out turtle nest excavation last week at Sandy Point in Swanton. Turtle nests are carefully excavated for two main reasons: the first is so that we can document the number of successful nests and hatchlings produced, and the second is to protect live young still in the ground from being eaten by predators. The threatened Eastern Spiny Softshell Turtle is the target species in this work, and three sites are managed for their nesting, with Sandy Point being historically the most important; however, other turtle species use the same beach, including Painted Turtles, Common Snapping Turtles, and Map Turtles, like the one seen here.

posts.c: Sonar with a side of squeaks! Bats have a remarkable ability called echolocation, which allows them to navigate in the dark by making high-pitched sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back. Essentially, they shout into the void and wait for the void to explain where everything is. Same. Still waiting… These sound waves help bats locate insects, avoid obstacles, and navigate their surroundings with impressive accuracy. They can even detect objects as small as human hair. Meanwhile, some humans have been known to walk into a glass door in broad daylight. One time. Moving on. Bats are an important part of many national park ecosystems, helping control insect populations and keeping nature ticking along after dark. So, the next time you hear a bat making noises, remember it isn’t screaming into the darkness. Well, it is, but it’s using a highly sophisticated biological sonar system. Screaming with purpose. Try it. Watch out for that door. NPS Photos: Bats flying in the darkness

I have been ice-obsessed since I was a kid crawling across the sea ice of the Arctic and running wild through the polar nights and endless summers. They allowed me to delve deeper into the raw beauty of places like Antarctica and return with scenes I still dream of. posts.c: Hanging peppers might look like an old-school gardening trick, but there’s some cool science behind it. When you hang peppers to dry, moisture gradually evaporates from their skin and inner tissues into the surrounding air. The key is airflow and low humidity, which help carry that moisture away so the peppers can dry more efficiently. As their water content drops, it becomes harder for many spoilage microbes to grow, helping preserve your harvest for longer. Here’s why the way you string them matters, too. Threading through the calyx, the leafy cap at the top of the pepper, helps avoid puncturing the fleshy fruit, where damaged tissue and trapped moisture can encourage rot. Give your peppers a dry, well-ventilated spot, and you’re using evaporation and moisture control to turn a fresh harvest into a longer-lasting supply of homegrown heat.

posts.c: After yesterday’s post, we were inundated with comments, well, two comments, about how we didn’t include a bat pic from Carlsbad Caverns in our Bat Week kickoff post. Also, someone just posted “waffles.” We see you, Leslie Knope. We’ve got a whole week to talk about bats, Jim, but we wanted to make sure and share a pic or two from Carlsbad to avoid more comments demanding a mention of one of the most famous areas for bats and people named Carl. Checks notes….hmmm, that’s not completely accurate. The Carl part. Anyways. So, here we are. And we agree that the park needs a shoutout. Carlsbad Caverns National Park is world-famous for its massive colonies of bats and nightly out-flight spectacles. For those wondering what an out-flight spectacle is, that’s when a massive colony of bats emerges in a synchronized evening exodus. Similar to when you deplane an aircraft, except everyone is a bat, the airport is a cave, and somehow all the passengers manage to leave at once without someone stand
posts.hd: Bat Week post adds Carlsbad Caverns bat photos

posts.c: 🦇 51 weeks of the year, bats are busy doing good by humans without many people ever realizing it. The last week of October, however, is that special 52nd week: Bat Week! That means it's time for us humans to say "thank you" to the bats! 🦇 If you're a professional bat biologist with Vermont Fish & Wildlife, every week is Bat Week, of course. The lucky few thank these glorious creatures by conducting cutting-edge telemetry research on their migratory patterns, or venturing deep underground to collect samples that will help us learn more about how bats are developing resilience against the devastating bat illness known as white-nose syndrome. But if you're not a bat biologist... what can YOU do for Bat Week? We recommend cleaning out your bat box! With bats leaving their summer roosts, you can tidy up a bat box at this time of year without worrying about disturbing the residents. Don't have a bat box? Well, you are in luck. Fall is a great time to pick a good spot and put up a bat box on

posts.c: The spirit bears of my new book Reverence. Over ten years ago, a @natgeo assignment sent me deep into the Great Bear Rainforest in search of the elusive spirit bear. At the time, big oil interests were pushing a pipeline from Canada’s Tar Sands to British Columbia, threatening the waterways that sustain the rainforest. First Nations communities were leading the fight against the project, and the magazine was after images that could rally the public behind them. Which is how I found myself crouched at the mossy edge of a cold stream, mesmerized as, just inches away, a spirit bear fished from the rushing waters. Under the guidance of @gitgaatspirit, I spent weeks in that mossy kingdom getting to know the wise little spirits that call it home. Soon after the story was finally published, the pipeline project was defeated. Reverence is now available in a limited print run, of which only a few thousand copies remain. posts.c: Most of us think of tulips as a spring flower. Emily von Trapp @vontrappflowers and Linda D'Arco @littlefarmhouseflowerspro built their businesses on proving otherwise. Emily grows 200,000 tulips a year in Waitsfield, Vermont, all of them in crates, in soil, blooming in the dead of a Vermont winter. Her first stems come around January 7th. Linda grows in Jay, New York, up in the Adirondacks. She forces hers hydroponically, and she started in the basement of a little farmhouse. They met in a Facebook group. Linda saw Emily's photo of tulips blooming in January and asked what the magic was. Then she talked Emily into teaching it. Today they run The Tulip Workshop together. Tune into episode 102 to learn: -What forcing actually is, explained for farmers and backyard gardeners both -What 5C and 9C mean, and why the variety matters as much as the number -Soil versus hydroponic, from two growers who each chose differently -The three mistakes that cost people their crop -Why your bulb order g

posts.c: Oh, so THAT’S what an “ongoing” work means…. Swing by “Catalyst: Art as Inquiry” before it closes on December 12, 2026. And even if you’d seen, Heimo Wallner’s “Last Note (Echo),” 2026 before, you’re going to want to take another look. From the artist: I draw, and this ongoing process manifests itself in piles of drawings, animations and when possible: room drawings—made quickly, with a clear deadline, these wall drawings force me to generate imagery on the spot and little strands of narratives crystallize, interweave, connect, and disrupt. They become rhythm, texture, ornament: wallpaper. The human condition is my quarry. Stupidity (my own and the general)—an endless source. The banal and the essential, daily news vs eternal truths, private painful secrets turn into practical jokes—catharsis and damnation all at once.

posts.c: When a fire broke out at our Drop-Off Center in Williston early Tuesday morning, our staff knew exactly what to do. They called the fire department, followed safety protocols, and kept everyone safe- all skills and confidence learned from staff trainings. Throughout the year, we occasionally close our facilities so our staff can receive training on emergency response, hazardous materials handling, and workplace safety. We know closures can be inconvenient, and we’re so grateful for your patience and understanding during those closures. This week was a reminder of why those trainings really matter. Thank you to our staff for their dedication and to our community for supporting the work it takes to keep our facilities safe.

posts.c: You don’t need a garden bed to grow potatoes, and the science behind it is pretty cool. A seed potato already contains the energy and nutrients needed to kickstart new growth. Once it sprouts, the roots pull water and nutrients from the soil, while the leaves capture sunlight and convert it into energy that fuels the development of new potatoes underground. The tricky part is creating the right environment for those tubers. We’re using @foxfarmsoilandfertilizer Ocean Forest soil to give each potato a consistent growing medium with nutrients to support early growth. Potatoes need consistent moisture, but soil that stays too wet can limit oxygen around the roots and encourage rot. Good drainage helps maintain that balance, which is why the container you choose can make a bigger difference than you might expect. That’s what makes this potato experiment so interesting. Different containers can change how quickly soil dries out, how much heat it holds, and how easily excess water escapes. B

posts.c: This planet is haunted! 👻 The ghosts of volcanic eruptions, asteroid strikes, and evaporated lakes here on Earth are visible in echoes seen from space. Explore some of the places on our planet still haunted by the past. A volcanic eruption about 4,000 years ago created the eerily named Deception Island. The horseshoe-shaped island is actually the exposed part of a volcano itself, while the harbor in its center is a phantom of that massive volcanic eruption. As the volcano’s magma chamber emptied, the sudden drop in pressure inside the volcano caused the top to collapse and form a caldera — now called Port Foster. Image description: Landsat 8 image of Deception Island. It is horseshoe shaped and mostly rocky brown. The thin arch of rock comes to a ridge that runs the length of the island, along its center, like a backbone. posts.c: Ever look at all the rain hitting your roof and wonder how much water you’re letting go to waste? A rainwater capture system puts that water to work. Every inch of rain falling on a 1,000-square-foot roof can produce around 600 gallons of water. Gutters collect the runoff and direct it into a system that can help keep your garden watered. The science is all about collecting and filtering water before it reaches storage. A leaf filter catches larger debris, while a first flush diverter sends the dirtiest initial runoff away from the tank. This matters because dust, bird droppings, and other contaminants can build up on your roof between rainfalls. Removing that initial runoff helps keep your stored water cleaner. This rainwater capture system stores up to 5,750 gallons across the property, with underground pipes directing collected water into a main 5,000-gallon tank. That stored supply can then help irrigate the garden during dry spells, reducing reliance on municipal water. It’s a pra

posts.c: We asked this 8-year-old to draw the famous “Cosmic Cliffs” hidden within the Carina Nebula, based on the famous James Webb Space Telescope image. The region is actually the edge of a gigantic, gaseous cavity within NGC 3324, roughly 7,600 light-years away. The cavernous area has been carved from the nebula by the intense ultraviolet radiation and stellar winds from extremely massive, hot, young stars located in the center of the bubble, above the area shown in this image. The high-energy radiation from these stars is sculpting the nebula’s wall by slowly eroding it away. Our artist managed to capture the beauty of this Webb image, along with her version of the telescope itself, a rocket ship, and there is even a cameo of "The Traveler" exploring the cosmos! Credit: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center Producer: Paul Morris Special thanks to Candy Jar, ASMR, and Donut Dan Music Credit: "Pizz with Pizzazz" by Bertrand Allagnat [SACEM] via Illustration Musicale [SACEM], Universal Productio

posts.c: Formerly Sugarsnap Farm, Wet Foot Farm is now owned and operated by Patrick Shafer, Jamie Cohen, and Abbey Duke. They’re one of seven farm operations growing food on land leased from the Intervale Center! Alongside produce for Sugarsnap Catering, the farm grows pawpaws—North America’s largest native edible fruit. With a creamy texture and hints of mango and banana, pawpaws naturally grow in moist forests and along waterways. Adapted to periodic flooding, these perennial trees support healthy ecosystems by stabilizing soil, reducing erosion, and providing wildlife habitat. Their resilience makes them a promising crop for climate-resilient agriculture. Pawpaw trees take several years to produce fruit, making growing them a long-term investment. Abbey Duke planted the original pawpaw trees in 2010 and in 2021, Patrick and Jamie began cultivating and planting more trees to meet growing demand, and they plan to continue expanding production in the coming years. posts.c: We are thrilled to share that @neiwpcc has named Mitzi Johnson as director of its Lake Champlain Programs Division and Director of the Lake Champlain Basin Program, effective October 13. Johnson brings more than two decades of public service, nonprofit leadership, and organizational strategy experience to the role. In these roles, Johnson will lead efforts to meet the challenges facing the Lake Champlain Basin through partnerships, science, and collaborative environmental management. During her 18-year tenure in the Vermont House of Representatives, Johnson served as Speaker of the House from 2017-2021 and held leadership positions on the House committees on agriculture and appropriations, building a strong background in water quality policy. Her career also includes extensive experience in consulting nonprofit organizations, research and educational institutions, and elected officials on leadership, management, and complex problem solving. posts.c: So @jacquesinthegarden stumbled across a mystery pomegranate tree growing near his house, and the fruit turned out to be the sweetest he’d ever tasted. The science comes down to genetics. Pomegranates grown from seed can have a unique combination of genes from their parent plants, so the fruit may taste completely different from what you’d expect. That’s why this mystery tree outperformed one he had intentionally grown for three years. If you find a pomegranate with incredible flavor, you’ll want to clone it rather than grow it from seed. Hardwood cuttings can develop roots and grow into genetically identical plants, preserving the traits that made the original fruit so good. Keeping those cuttings warm while providing indirect light can help encourage root development, especially during cooler weather. And here’s the fun part: birds like crows can spread seeds to new places, creating unexpected seedlings throughout a neighborhood. You might not know what you’re growing until it fruits

posts.c: Nice day for a WINOOSKI wedding! 😍✨ Such a pleasure photographing Emily and Joe’s wedding on a gorgeous, late-summer day on (literally!) the Winooski River in Vermont. Narrowing the full gallery down to just a few select photos to share on Instagram was not easy! Wedding photography is a TEST of all your skills as a photographer: • shifting your composition and lighting constantly, based on scene and subject • directing subjects while allowing for natural expression, finding moments to make art • remaining present while anticipating the next 5 minutes, knowing when to linger vs. move on … all while staying! out! of! the! way! during a 6-8 hour shindig. I’m super proud of this gallery of images I produced. Photography is a dream job! Reality is remarkable! - - - venue: @waterworksvt

posts.c: We created a fleet of no-cost, seriously spooky, DIY witches brooms, with cuttings from our own yard.⠀⠀ 🧹 ⠀⠀ Start by cutting small bundles of ornamental grass and hang them upside down to dry (you can skip the drying part). Cut branches to size (we got ours from our birch tree) and on one end wrap and knot twine - making sure to leave a 6” tail. Then, center the branch in a grass bundle before wrapping the grass with twine to keep it in place. Use the tail to tie off. Trim the grass to your desired length. Last, use a hook or just tie string around the other end of the branch to hang. ⠀⠀ 🧹 ⠀⠀ We love the look and it was the perfect project to get us started on a very spooky exterior 🧙‍♀️⠀⠀ •⠀⠀ #renovationhusbands #diy #diydecor #halloween #halloweendecor diyhalloween

posts.c: 🔎 Can you spot the lingcod? This lingcod may be guarding eggs. Males stay with them for up to two months until they hatch. Every seafood meal is connected to a special place like this one. The eelgrass meadows where young Dungeness crabs hide until they’re big enough. The kelp forests where juvenile rockfish stay safe among the fronds. The sandy seafloor that looks empty to us but is teeming with life. And of course the coral reefs that support a quarter of all marine species. These ocean habitats face many pressures, and how seafood is caught and farmed is one of them. Choosing sustainable seafood is one thing we all can do to help protect these special places. 💬 Comment “guide” and check your DMs. #NationalSeafoodMonth #SeafoodMonth #SustainableSeafood #SeafoodWatch #MontereyBayAquarium

posts.c: 🍂 Fall tick season is in full swing, and adult black-legged ticks (deer ticks) are active now. These are the ticks that can spread Lyme disease and other diseases to both people and pets. Stock up on flea and tick prevention, treatment and removal products, all 20% OFF in stores through October! The sale includes great options like the Tick Mitt and Seresto collars. Our Seresto collar price is already lower than what you’ll find at most retailers, so with an additional 20% off, now is a great time to pick one up. Stop by either Pet Food Warehouse location and be prepared for fall tick season while shopping local! Our staff is happy to help you pick out the products that will work for you and your pets. For more general info ticks in Vermont, visit: https://www.healthvermont.gov/disease-control/tick-bite-illnesses/prevent-tick-bites-tickborne-diseases

posts.c: Best of my time in west mt airy 🩷 the most magical cottagey rowhouse on the most charming street- I put a lot of love into this place to make it feel like home for me- painted the whole dang thing, replaced the light fixtures, planted a whole bunch of plants, and more! I enjoyed her for 2.5 years but it was time for change! I went through a big breakup here- my first and only relationship that lasted 8 years. I lived here alone for a year and a half, becoming a single cat mommy of two, while I healed and found my way back to myself, found new hobbies (tennis, rock climbing, knitting, golfing, following baseball again), prioritizing my friendships and making new ones, learning how to spend comfortable time alone and figure things out for myself after living with someone for so long. I imagine I’ll find my way back to mt airy since I love her so much, but for now I’m back in the city and excited to decorate my new solo (!!!) apt and for all that comes next 💖

posts.c: Brewing up new stars 🪄 @NASAWebb’s unique view of the stellar nursery known as NGC 7129 reveals numerous stars formerly hidden in this cosmic cauldron. Stars begin their life in cold, dense regions of dust and gas, hiding from view of most telescopes. Webb’s high degree of infrared sensitivity allows astronomers to peer through dust to study these baby stars. In this image, we can see stars in various stages of development. The most mature and massive (about 5-8x the mass of our Sun) is the region’s bright central star. In the cavity on the left, appearing in gold, is the largest demonstration of its impact. The outflows from an earlier stage in the star’s development carve into the dense molecular cloud of hydrogen, and combine with the star’s light, causing it to glow. The region on the right, represented in red, hides much younger objects than those on the left: protostars. posts.c: Checking in on my Peace Lily - one of my first plants! - Light analysis: in a white LED grow light context, you need to specify the strength (FC or µmol/s/m² is fine) and the duration - you can calculate the DLI by multiplying the strength and the duration (along with the appropriate conversions) - For this plant: 90 FC x 14 hours gives you a DLI of 0.8 mol/day, which is quite low but clearly still enough to produce some flowers. With a higher DLI, my plant would have probably produced more flowers but I'm happy with where this plant is and how it has grown for now - The spent leaves on a peace lily don't tend to fall off on their own like a pothos or philodendron so you should regularly cut them off once they're fully dead - staying on top of it will allow space for new leaves to grow (mine has become a bit crowded!) - #houseplantjournal #peacelily #spathyphyllum

held.c: This is Saraya. She has always doted on her baby brother Alexander, but when she started repeatedly licking and nudging the six-month-old and becoming distressed, her family knew something was off. Later, Alexander began crying inconsolably, and while fussiness isn’t unusual for babies, this combined with Saraya’s behavior prompted the family to seek help immediately. After being rushed to the hospital, Alexander was found to have a dangerously high heart rate at 280 beats per minute and was diagnosed with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. With treatment he has been able to maintain a safe heart rate since. “She’s not a trained assistance dog in any way,” Saraya’s human said. “But she was trying to tell us that Alexander needed help. I will be forever grateful to her.” 15/10 (credit @countygazette)

held.c: Canadians, incensed by U.S. President Donald Trump’s repeated threats to annex Canada as the 51st state, have boycotted or cut back on travel to the U.S., crippling the border towns that have long depended on their business. Tensions between the two nations peaked in August, when trade negotiations collapsed and Trump imposed staggering 50 percent tariffs on hundreds of Canadian goods. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney struck back with his own retaliatory tariffs, matching Trump’s “dollar-for-dollar” and announcing that Canada will pursue a closer relationship with the European Union. In the towns and villages in Vermont’s Northeast Kingdom, where daily life is shaped by proximity to the border, something much more profound — and less easily measured — is at stake. On Canusa Street, some American homes fly Canadian flags from their porches as a message of apology to their neighbors. Rest easy, Captain. We have the helm. ✨ Here is Webb’s look at Westerlund 1, a super star cluster - one of the closest clusters of its kind. Super star clusters are young and contain more than 10,000 times the mass of the Sun packed into a small volume. Westerlund 1 is the most massive yet identified in our galaxy, with 50,000 to 100,000 times the mass of the Sun contained within a region less than six light-years across. Super star clusters are one of the most extreme environments in which stars and planets can form. Because our galaxy is past its peak of star formation, and because such stars live relatively short lives, only a few of these clusters still exist to give us clues to that past era. Image credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, M. Zamani (ESA/Webb), M. G. Guarcello (INAF-OAPA) and the EWOCS team Image description: A quote by Captain Jean-Luc Picard, played by Patrick Stewart. In 1903, Theodore Roosevelt and naturalist John Muir embarked on a three-day wilderness trip in Yosemite National Park. They camped the first night at the Mariposa Grove under the Grizzly Giant. The second night was spent near Sentinel Dome during a snowstorm. The third night was at the edge Bridalveil Meadow in Yosemite Valley. After the trip, Roosevelt said of Yosemite, “There can be nothing in the world more beautiful than the Yosemite, the groves of the giant sequoias...our people should see to it that they are preserved for their children and their Children’s children forever...” Born on October 27, 1858, Theodore Roosevelt, the 26th president of the United States, left a lasting mark on America’s public lands. During his presidency, he established five national parks, designated 18 national monuments, created 51 federal bird reservations, and protected approximately 230 million acres of public land for future generations. Today, you can celebrate his birthday by visiting a nation

Three days before the Vermont Symphony Orchestra takes the stage at the Flynn, join VSO Music Director Andrew Crust and composer James Stewart at the Venetian Soda Lounge for a lively happy hour exploring the music on our October 31 program, The Sorcerer’s Apprentice. What if you could turn a chicken into part of the process of growing a giant pumpkin? When Gucci, one of my original hens, passed away, I buried her beneath an Atlantic Giant pumpkin. Here’s the cool part: as bacteria and fungi break down organic matter, they recycle nutrients back into the soil. Plants can’t use all those nutrients immediately, though. Decomposition transforms them into forms roots can absorb, making decomposers an incredibly important part of a healthy garden. But growing a giant pumpkin takes more than nutrient-rich soil. I buried the vines so more nodes could develop roots, giving the plant additional access to water and nutrients. I removed competing flowers and fruits to focus the plant’s resources on one pumpkin, then added sand and plywood underneath to support its growing weight. Even with all those tricks, powdery mildew showed up and eventually slowed its growth. That’s what makes giant vegetables so fascinating: genetics, photosynthesis, growing conditions,

held.c: Born in a small country town in New England and into a musical family, Grammy-nominated songwriter @reedfoehl started out as a street singer on the streets of Boston and has gone on to record and release over 11 studio albums that have garnered him national attention with numerous placements in film and television and as a touring singer-songwriter. Foehl writes songs like postcards from the long way home- Weathered, honest and quietly devastating. Rooted in American folk, his music carries the weight of loss, love and survival, told with a voice that sounds lived-in and unafraid. There’s a grit in the stories, grace in the melodies, and a deep human tenderness running through it all.​ Friday, October 30th 6-8PM. Reservations Recommended. This ticketed, multi-course, family-style meal is a celebration the flavors of fall as part of @slowfoodvt Chicory Month. 10 years ago today, we received a mention from a man named Brant. What followed was an interaction that has quite literally changed my life. Brant received a lot of criticism for his words that day, but 2016 was a different, more graceful internet, and he rolled with the punches. He wore the “they’re good dogs Brent” merch we sent him, his Simpson’s themed wedding cake featured Santa’s Little Helper holding a sign featuring the phrase, and best of all, 2 years later, Brant got a dog. Completing potentially the most wholesome, full circle meme to ever exist. We haven’t heard from him in a few years, but Brant, wherever you are, give Charlie a hug from us ❤️
